A feature release. The theme is **other machines** — Claude Code sessions
running somewhere else now get orbs, and a chat panel that shows the real
conversation rather than a model's account of it. Alongside that: a
deterministic fix for Claude Desktop profile logins going to the wrong profile,
a chat panel you can resize and that remembers its size per agent, and a test
suite that went from measuring a fifth of this app to measuring all of it.

Still a beta. Remote Control is macOS-only, and the *Known limitations* section
below is not boilerplate — read it before relying on any of this.

## New: Claude Code sessions on your other machines

If you run Claude Code on more than one machine — a desktop at home, a server, a
laptop you left on — those sessions can now appear as orbs here, badged `⇄`, and
you can send them instructions from anywhere. **No port to open, no tunnel, and
nothing installed on the other machine.** It works from a hotel exactly as it
does from your desk.

The requirement is that the far session has **Remote Control on**
(`claude --remote-control`, or `/remote-control` in a running session) — the same
sessions you could already reach from your phone. A session without it stays
invisible here, which is also how you keep one private.

**Why it costs something.** Anthropic's Remote Control relay has no third-party
API, so Buddy cannot ask it anything. What it *can* do is start a hidden Claude
Code session of its own with Remote Control on, because such a session is handed
tools that reach the account's other sessions wherever they run. That session is
the relay: your own account, no server of ours in the path. It also means the
feature spends your quota while it is up — which is why it is off until you turn
it on, only starts when something asks, and shuts itself down again when idle.

Turn it on in **Settings → Other machines**:

- **Account** — which Claude Code config directory the relay signs in as. Remote
  Control only sees sessions on the same account, so pick the one your other
  machines use. A second account goes under **Claude Code profiles** first.
- **Stop the relay after** — how long it may sit unused before shutting down. It
  restarts by itself next time you open or send to a remote session.

Nothing starts merely because the switch is on. **Connect to other machines** in
the tray menu, the button in Settings, or just opening a remote session's chat
brings the relay up; orbs appear a few seconds later.

### The panel shows the real conversation — if the far machine also runs Buddy

This is the part worth understanding, because the two cases behave differently
and the panel says which one you are in.

**Both machines running Claude Buddy: a live view.** The panel shows that
session's own conversation, the same words the person in front of it sees,
because the Buddy over there reads the transcript off its own disk and sends it
across verbatim. You can scroll back through it. What you type goes into that
session's terminal, so **every slash command works** — `/color`, `/rename`, all
of them — because the CLI's own command handler runs them. Updates arrive as the
session works, not only when it finishes.

**Only this machine running Buddy: a messaging channel**, which is what this was
always, and the panel labels it in as many words. Without a Buddy on the far
side there is no way to read a file there; the only channel is peer messaging,
which reaches the far session's *model* rather than its terminal. So what comes
back is a reply that model composed **for you** — its own account of its
conversation rather than the conversation. That is the transport, not
politeness: it was measured being asked not to summarise, and it paraphrased
anyway. Claude Code's built-ins (`/compact`, `/color`, `/agents`) cannot work at
all this way, so the panel asks each session which *custom* commands it has and
offers only those — and offers nothing until it answers, rather than offering
commands that would fail.

| | Live view | Messaging (fallback) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you see | the far session's transcript, verbatim | a reply its model wrote for you |
| Scrollback | yes | no |
| Slash commands | all of them, built-ins included | custom only |
| Where your text goes | that session's input line | that session's model context |

**The live view is verify-or-refuse.** Every piece of transcript that crosses
the wire carries a SHA-256 of what it should be, because the thing relaying it is
a language model pasting base64 it cannot read. A piece that arrives altered is
re-requested twice and then **refused** — the panel shows an error and none of
the transcript. It deliberately does *not* fall back to the model-written
version, which would substitute a summary at exactly the moment integrity
failed.

**Identity is joined, not guessed.** Two remote sessions sharing a name make the
panel refuse rather than pick one, because picking would be right half the time
and wrong invisibly — showing you someone's other conversation.

One thing a remote orb cannot know is **which computer it is on**: a peer is
reported as a name, a kind and a status, with no hostname anywhere, so the title
is that name alone. Its **colour** it does know, by asking once per session per
run; until it answers, the orb takes a colour derived from its name so several
remote orbs are still tellable apart.

## Fixed: Claude Desktop links went to the wrong profile

If you use coloured Claude Desktop profiles, this is the release you want.

The reported symptoms — profile switching "sometimes opens them in the wrong
profile", "sometimes I can't login", "sometimes makes me log in multiple times" —
are **one deterministic bug**, not three intermittent ones.

Claude Desktop declares two URL schemes: `claude:` for deep links and
`msauth.com.anthropic.claudefordesktop:` for the Microsoft sign-in callback.
Every tinted profile clone is a byte-identical copy of `Claude.app` (that is what
keeps its keychain access working), so every clone declares the same schemes
under the same bundle id — and macOS records a URL handler by bundle id alone.
On the reporting machine three bundles answered to that id, and the one macOS
picked was `/Applications/Claude.app`, which is never the bundle a coloured
profile runs from. A LaunchServices launch carries no profile environment, so the
sign-in callback opened **Default**.

Signing in to any non-Default profile therefore sent the token to Default: a
Default window appeared (wrong profile), the profile you were signing into never
completed (can't log in), and you retried (log in repeatedly). It looked
intermittent only because signing in to Default itself works fine.

Claude Buddy now claims both schemes and forwards each link to one specific
instance, addressed by its clone's **path** — unique per profile even though the
bundle id is not. Nothing is claimed until you actually have more than one
profile, and a Settings toggle hands the scheme back. Verified with the same
process probe before and after: before, a second Claude started under
`/Applications` and the Board profile never got the link; after, nothing else
started and the link reached the profile it belonged to.

Two related bugs, both of which made this look random:

- **Deleted profile clones never unregistered.** Removing a profile deleted the
  directory but left the bundle registered, so a clone deleted months ago was
  still claiming `claude:`.
- **Ambiguous launches.** Launching Default without a clone passed a bundle id
  every clone answers to, so macOS could start a clone instead. It is now always
  launched by path.

**Also fixed: Dock icon tinting had silently stopped working.** The success
marker was written *before* the icon was actually set, so a refusal — the
App Management permission, which an unsigned rebuild silently invalidates — was
recorded as success, and the clone was then treated as correctly coloured
permanently and never retried.

## New: a chat panel you can resize, that stays that size

Drag any edge or corner of the chat panel and it resizes; new turns then scroll
inside it rather than growing it out from under your hands. Message bubbles use
the extra room instead of staying at a fixed width.

**The size belongs to the agent, not to the window.** Each agent reopens at
whatever you last dragged its panel to, across restarts, and an agent you have
never resized still opens at the shipped 340×420. Keyed by agent rather than by
session id, since Claude Code mints a new session id every conversation and a
size saved under one would never be found again.

## New: slash-command autocomplete, and pasting pictures

**Autocomplete.** Typing `/` in the panel's input box now brings up the same kind
of suggestion list the terminal draws — filtering as you type, ↑/↓ to move,
Tab/Enter to accept, Escape to dismiss. The list merges each CLI's fixed
commands with a live scan of your own `.claude/commands/`, `.claude/skills/` and
`~/.codex/prompts/`, following the precedence each CLI documents. Local Claude
Code and Codex sessions only — a gateway conversation has no command grammar on
the far end to suggest.

**Pasting a picture.** Cmd/Ctrl+V with an image on the clipboard now reaches a
local Claude Code or Codex session: the picture is written to a temp PNG and its
path typed into the terminal line as its own word, which is the same thing that
happens when you drag a file into that terminal. `tmux send-keys` can only type
characters, so this is the only route there is. Pasting text is unchanged, and
OpenClaw gateway sessions still get plain text paste — `chat.send` carries a
string, and a local file path means nothing at the other end of a websocket.

## New: a beating heart on heartbeat-driven sessions

An OpenClaw gateway wakes each agent on a timer to do background work, in the
agent's *own main session*. On a gateway with eight agents that is eight orbs
lighting up together every half hour with nobody on the other end — and an orb
that just lit up reads as somebody waiting for you, which is the one thing these
are not. They now wear a beating heart, and **Settings → OpenClaw agents → Show
heartbeat sessions** turns them off entirely.

The heart marks **where a heartbeat lands**, not which individual turns were one.
The gateway does not report heartbeats at all — measured against a real gateway,
84 sessions across 8 agents, and none of the six candidate signals held. Two
honest consequences: an agent whose heartbeat is switched *off* still gets a
heart (whether it is enabled is config behind a scope this app deliberately does
not request), and a heartbeat retargeted at a channel is not marked. Both err in
the direction that cannot say anything false about who can read a conversation.

## Fixed: orbs that went missing

Three separate ways a session could be running with nothing on screen to say so:

- **Concurrent background sessions collapsed into one orb.** Agent View
  background sessions share their parent process's pid rather than getting one of
  their own, and the dedupe rule that removes stale `/clear` leftovers was
  grouping by pid — so several genuinely separate, concurrently running sessions
  became one orb. Confirmed on a real machine: one pid owning four status files
  with distinct titles, transcripts, and in one case a different directory.
- **A resumed background job lost its orb entirely.** A job keeps the id it was
  created with while the work moves to a session with a new id, and the lookup
  was deriving one from the other — a relationship that only holds for a job's
  *first* session. Verified A/B against a live session: 0 orbs drawn before, 1
  after.
- **The macOS hook recorded the wrong process.** It took the first ancestor
  owning a terminal, so a forked session recorded the viewer's pid and a dead
  session looked alive forever. Windows' hook was already correct.

## Under the hood: the test suite now measures the whole app

Line coverage went from **22.5% to 100%** (11,057 lines), branches from 16.1% to
89%, across all four automated suites — and three defects in the *measurement*
were fixed, so the number means what it says. Chief among them: the two coverage
engines disagreed about method-level exclusions, and 157 exclusions were being
silently added back into the denominator.

The rule kept honest throughout: an exclusion goes only on code a headless CI
runner genuinely cannot execute, every exclusion carries a comment naming the
specific thing that cannot run, and **"it's UI" is not a reason** — the UI suite
drives real Avalonia headlessly. Where a method could not be run, the *decision*
it makes was pulled out into a pure function and tested instead.

This is not a user-facing feature, but it is why several of the fixes above exist
at all: sweeping the orb-geometry cases a second time with the shape anchored
found two bugs that had shipped uncovered, both invisible while the shape was
always drawn in the middle of the screen.

## Fixed, smaller

- The auto-arranged shape's saved position now survives a restart. It was
  declared on the settings model but never actually written or read, so it worked
  for the life of one process and silently reset on relaunch.
- Dragging the arranged cluster somewhere else now sticks, instead of being
  undone by the next orb that joins or leaves.
- A team fanned out from a lead in a screen corner no longer draws every member
  on the same pixel.
- Thirty orbs piled into a corner now actually untangle.

## Which file do I want

| Platform | Download |
| --- | --- |
| macOS, Apple silicon (M1 and later) | `ClaudeBuddy-0.4.2-beta-osx-arm64.dmg` |
| macOS, Intel | `ClaudeBuddy-0.4.2-beta-osx-x64.dmg` |
| Windows 10/11, 64-bit | `ClaudeBuddy-0.4.2-beta-win-x64-setup.exe` |

The `ClaudeBuddySpeech-0.4.2-beta-*.zip` assets are the optional high-quality
voice engine. **You do not download these yourself** — the app fetches the right
one when you turn the setting on. They are published here because that is where
it looks.

The .NET runtime is bundled; nothing else is needed. `SHA256SUMS.txt` covers
every file — verify with `shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS.txt` on macOS or
`Get-FileHash <file> -Algorithm SHA256` on Windows.

## Upgrading from 0.4.1-beta

**macOS**: replace the app in Applications. The signing identity is unchanged, so
Automation permission and click-to-focus carry over.

If you use coloured Claude Desktop profiles, this release claims the `claude:`
and `msauth…` URL schemes on first launch (only when you have more than one
profile) — that is the profile-login fix above, and **Settings → Claude Desktop**
hands the scheme back if you would rather it did not. Tinted icons that had
silently stopped applying are rebuilt; if the tint still does not take, grant
Claude Buddy **App Management** in System Settings → Privacy & Security, which an
unsigned rebuild invalidates.

**Windows**: run the new setup over the old one; it upgrades in place and leaves
your hook configuration alone. Nothing in this release's headline features
reaches Windows yet — see below.

Remote Control is **off by default** and starts nothing until you both turn it on
and ask it to connect.

Hooks are read once at session start, so **restart any open sessions** after
installing or updating.

## Installing fresh

**macOS** — open the DMG, drag Claude Buddy to Applications, then double-click
**Install Claude Code Hooks.command**. Launch from Applications; nothing appears
in the Dock and no window opens, which is correct — look in the menu bar.

**Windows** — run the setup. Per-user, so no UAC prompt. Leave both checkboxes
ticked; tick **"Wire hooks for Claude Code running inside WSL"** too if you use
it.

### The hook step is not optional

Claude Buddy learns about your sessions from a hook that Claude Code (and, for
Codex sessions, Codex) runs. Until it is wired in, the app starts and runs
correctly and shows **nothing at all**. The installers offer to wire it up; let
them. Existing settings are backed up first, and re-running repairs rather than
duplicating.

## Known limitations

- **Remote Control is macOS only.** The relay is tmux-shaped; a Windows
  transport is tracked separately and is gated off rather than half-working.
- **The Claude Desktop URL-routing fix is macOS only** — it is a fix for macOS
  LaunchServices behaviour, and there is no Windows equivalent of the bug.
- **No streaming without a Buddy on the far side.** In messaging mode, a reply
  arrives when the remote session chooses to send it. The substitutes are the
  orb pulsing, a "…is working" line, and polling tightening to 5 seconds while
  something is in flight.
- **Two relays running at once is not fully verified.** One account was
  exercised end to end against a real second Mac; a second local account is
  blocked by Claude Code's own unfinished first-run setup, which this now detects
  and explains in seconds rather than hanging.
- **Enabling Remote Control publishes the relay to your own Remote Control
  surface**, so Buddy's hidden session appears in the list on your phone. It is
  named after itself rather than disguised.
- **Setting a remote session's colour is fixture-covered, not verified live** —
  proving it meant changing a colour on somebody's working session.
- **The heartbeat's beat has never been watched moving on a screen.** It is
  asserted as a curve and rendered as a still frame; the label-matching branch is
  untested against a real payload, because the gateway's own heartbeat job sits
  behind a scope this app does not hold.
- **A pasted picture's transcript round-trip is assumed, not verified.** Whether
  Claude Code records the typed line verbatim has not been confirmed against a
  real captured transcript row. Worst case the message appears twice in the panel
  for a moment and then corrects itself — not a crash, not a lost message.
- **The resize path has not run on Windows or Linux.** It avoids platform APIs
  deliberately (the obvious system call is a silent no-op on macOS, which is why
  the drag is hand-rolled), so it should work — but "should" is the honest word.
- **Windows installers are unsigned** — SmartScreen warns; choose **More info →
  Run anyway**. macOS builds are signed and notarized and open normally.
- A session killed with Ctrl+C at a permission prompt can still leave its orb
  stuck on amber. Right-click → *Reset this session to idle* clears it.

`docs/remote-control-findings.md`, `docs/claude-desktop-url-routing-findings.md`
and `docs/openclaw-findings.md` record what was actually measured versus assumed,
in more detail than fits here — including, in the first of those, three cases
where a test passed while measuring nothing and the stronger version caught a
real failure.
